class="css-1e96uhg"><header><h2 class="css-ba3xht">Key takeaways</h2><div class="css-t9podz"><ul>
<li>A brand-name drug is the original version of a medication that’s FDA-approved to treat a specific condition. Generics contain exact copies of the active ingredient in the original branded drug (an active ingredient is what makes a drug work). </li>



<li>Generics are widely proven to be as safe and effective as brand-name medications. But they may have different inactive ingredients that can affect how well the drug works for you.</li>



<li>Most generics are sold under the name of their active ingredient, but some drugmakers may sell them under trade names. These drugs are called “branded generics,” and are still treated as generic drugs for medical and insurance purposes. </li>
</ul></div></header><section></section></article></div></div></div></div><div class="css-168l8xe"><aside class="css-zezy6m" data-testid="sticky-inline-ad" data-sticky="false"><div class="css-1xdhyk6"><div class="css-1v9qaky" data-empty="true"><div class="css-111xg9d"><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div id="inline2__slot" data-adbridg-ad-class="inline2__slot" data-ad="true" data-adbridg-skvp="" class="css-fo4nvu"></div></div></div></aside></div></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="generic-vs-name-brand" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="generic-vs-name-brand">Is there a difference between the generic and name-brand versions of a drug?</a></div></h2></div><span style="font-size:0;line-height:0"></span><div><p>There are no major differences between generic and brand-name versions of a drug. </p></div><div><p>Generic medications go through testing for quality, strength, purity, and potency to show effectiveness before approval by the FDA. They must have the same active ingredient and provide the same benefits.</p></div><div><p>Although some generic drugs may look different than the brand-name versions, these differences don’t change how well the drug works. </p></div><div><div data-testid="widget" data-widget="109876-end-of-section-link"><div><span style="font-size:0;line-height:0"></span><div class="css-1mjkuo7"><strong><span class="css-tkdora">»</span>Need to identify a tablet or capsule?</strong><a class="css-1jvleci" rel="endofsectionlink noopener noreferrer" href="https://www.healthline.com/pill-identifier" data-prompt="Need to identify a tablet or capsule?">Use Healthline's Pill Identifier to find drug names and images.</a></div></div></div></div></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="effectiveness" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="effectiveness">Why don’t generic drugs work for me?</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Generic medications might contain different inactive ingredients than the brand-name version, including fillers, binders, and artificial coloring. </p></div><div><p>For most people, inactive ingredients won’t change how well a drug works. But some health factors (like an allergy or intolerance to an ingredient) can affect how your body responds to a medication.</p></div><div><p>Common inactive ingredients in medications include:</p></div><div><ul><li>lactose</li><li>corn starch</li><li>food dyes, including <a href="https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/red-dye-40" class="content-link css-kxhged">Red 40</a> (also known as Allura Red)</li></ul></div><div><p>If you feel like a generic drug doesn’t work as well as the brand-name version, talk with your doctor or pharmacist. They can help you compare the drug’s ingredients and determine whether any might be <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/drug-interactions" class="content-link css-kxhged">interacting</a> with your personal health factors. </p></div><div><blockquote class="is-layout-flow wp-block-quote-is-layout-flow css-adix5v"><strong>Medical Perspective</strong><p>For most people, generic drugs work just as well as brand-name ones. They’re made with the same active ingredient and are tested to show that they work the same way in your body. If you’re not sure whether a brand-name or generic drug is best for you, talk with your doctor. </p><p class="has-text-align-left">— <a href="https://www.healthline.com/reviewers/stan-saji-pharmd-mba-rph" class="content-link css-kxhged">Stan Saji, PharmD, MBA, RPh</a></p><p><a href="https://care.healthline.com/find-care/specialty/primary-care-doctors" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">Find a primary care doctor in your area today.</a></p><p><em><sub>Quotes represent the opinions of our medical experts. Before that, he was a clinical content editor after serving for a decade as DiabetesMine's managing editor, tapping into his life with type 1 diabetes since childhood to write and advocate for the Diabetes Community. With a journalism degree from Oakland University, Mike has 25 years of experience at daily, weekly, and specialty print and digital media publications. When not working, Mike may be researching his family history, exploring vintage typewriters and rotary phones, or hanging out in Southeast Michigan with his wife and dog.\u003c/p\u003e\r\n\r\n\u003ch2 data-pm-slice=\"1 1 []\"\u003eMy Editorial Approach\u003c/h2\u003e\r\n\u003cp data-pm-slice=\"1 1 []\"\u003eI believe that healthcare information should be two things: accurate and accessible. By bridging the gap between science-based truth and human-centered storytelling, I create content that ranges from rigorous clinical editing to personal narratives. Whether I’m breaking down complex data or sharing a lived experience, my goal remains the same: to empower readers at every stage of their health journey.\u003c/p\u003e\r\n\r\n\u003ch2 data-pm-slice=\"1 1 []\"\u003eFeatured Articles\u003c/h2\u003e\r\n\u003ch3\u003eCan AI Help You Manage Diabetes?\u003c/h3\u003e\r\nAI is changing the world and how we interact within it. Medically reviewed by Stan Saji, PharmD, MBA, RPh — Written by Malini Ghoshal, RPh, MS — Updated on February 16, 2026 Generic vs. name brand Effectiveness Generics and brand-name versions FAQ Takeaway Key takeaways A brand-name drug is the original version of a medication that’s FDA-approved to treat a specific condition. Generics contain exact copies of the active ingredient in the original branded drug (an active ingredient is what makes a drug work). Generics are widely proven to be as safe and effective as brand-name medications. But they may have different inactive ingredients that can affect how well the drug works for you. Most generics are sold under the name of their active ingredient, but some drugmakers may sell them under trade names. These drugs are called “branded generics,” and are still treated as generic drugs for medical and insurance purposes. Is there a difference between the generic and name-brand versions of a drug? There are no major differences between generic and brand-name versions of a drug. Generic medications go through testing for quality, strength, purity, and potency to show effectiveness before approval by the FDA. They must have the same active ingredient and provide the same benefits. Although some generic drugs may look different than the brand-name versions, these differences don’t change how well the drug works. » Need to identify a tablet or capsule? Use Healthline's Pill Identifier to find drug names and images. Why don’t generic drugs work for me? Generic medications might contain different inactive ingredients than the brand-name version, including fillers, binders, and artificial coloring. For most people, inactive ingredients won’t change how well a drug works. But some health factors (like an allergy or intolerance to an ingredient) can affect how your body responds to a medication. Common inactive ingredients in medications include: lactose corn starch food dyes, including Red 40 (also known as Allura Red) If you feel like a generic drug doesn’t work as well as the brand-name version, talk with your doctor or pharmacist. They can help you compare the drug’s ingredients and determine whether any might be interacting with your personal health factors. Medical Perspective For most people, generic drugs work just as well as brand-name ones. They’re made with the same active ingredient and are tested to show that they work the same way in your body. If you’re not sure whether a brand-name or generic drug is best for you, talk with your doctor. — Stan Saji, PharmD, MBA, RPh Find a primary care doctor in your area today. Quotes represent the opinions of our medical experts. All content is strictly informational and should not be considered medical advice. Common generic drugs and brand-name equivalents The table below lists some commonly prescribed generic drugs and their brand-name versions. When discussing medications, healthcare providers may use the names of branded and generic versions interchangeably. Generic medications Brand-name versions apixaban • Eliquis • Eliquis Sprinkle atorvastatin • Lipitor • Atorvaliq levothyroxine • Synthroid • Unithroid • Levoxyl lisinopril • Zestril • Prinivil albuterol • Ventolin • Proair omeprazole • Prilosec • Prilosec OTC dextroamphetamine/amphetamine salts • Adderall • Adderall XR acetaminophen • Tylenol ibuprofen • Motrin • Advil Frequently asked questions Below are some frequently asked questions about generic and brand-name drugs. Why do branded medicines cost so much more than generics? Brand-name medications are new discoveries developed through research and clinical trials. New drugs go through years of testing on animals and humans to prove they are safe and effective before they are ready for us to use. This takes a lot of money, so brand companies get patent and exclusivity protection from competition for 20 years. The manufacturer of the brand can set any price for that medication to profit from their new discovery. Who decides if I get brand-name drugs or generics when I get a prescription filled? Some medications are only available in a brand-name version. But if a medication has a generic version, many states have laws that require pharmacists to switch to a generic when one is available. In most states, pharmacy staff must notify you about switching to the generic. Your doctor can write “do not substitute,” “dispense as written,” or “brand medically necessary” to avoid generic switching. You can refuse a generic substitution. But if you have insurance, only the cost of the generic medication may be covered. Most insurance companies have drug formularies or lists of approved medications. How to tell if your insurance or Medicare plan covers a generic or brand-name drug Most insurance companies, including Medicare Part D drug plans, have a formulary, or list of preferred drugs, in a step system of five or six tiers The lower tiers have preferred generics and are usually just a few dollars. The highest tier has specialty brand medications that usually require prior authorization or approval from your insurance company because they are expensive. Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance usually requires a generic substitution if one’s available. If you want a brand when a generic is available, you may have to pay out of pocket or use a third-party savings program. » MORE: Search for your medication on Optum Perks to see available coupons and download a free Optum Perks discount card. Takeaway Brand and generic medications must prove they are both safe and effective for FDA approval. If you choose to take a brand medication over a generic, your insurance may require you to pay full price. Generics are the less expensive option in most cases. For certain medical conditions, your doctor may prefer sticking with a brand to keep your levels steady. Some medications, like blood thinners or seizure drugs, have a very small safe dosing range. If you’re switching between a brand-name and a generic version of these, talk with your doctor. They may want to monitor you more closely to make sure the medication continues to work well for you. Your pharmacist can answer any concerns you have about brand or generic medications. To learn more about generic medications, you can visit the FDA website here or call 1-888-INFO-FDA. You can also qualify if you have certain health conditions or <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-eligibility-disability" class="content-link css-kxhged">disabilities</a>.</p><p>Medicare is divided into a few “parts.” Each part of Medicare covers different healthcare needs. Currently, the parts of Medicare include:<br></p><ul><li><strong>Medicare Part A.</strong> <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-part-a" class="content-link css-kxhged">Medicare Part A</a> is hospital insurance. It covers you during short-term, inpatient stays in hospitals and skilled nursing facilities or for some in-home services like limited home healthcare or hospice.</li><li><strong>Medicare Part B.</strong> <a href="http://healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-part-b" class="content-link css-kxhged">Medicare Part B</a> is medical insurance that covers everyday care needs like doctor's appointments, therapist visits, medical equipment, and urgent care visits.</li><li><strong>Medicare Part C.</strong> <a href="http://healthline.com//health/medicare/medicare-part-c" class="content-link css-kxhged">Medicare Part C</a> is also called Medicare Advantage. These plans combine the coverage of parts A and B into a single plan. Medicare Advantage plans are offered by private insurance companies and are overseen by Medicare.</li><li><strong>Medicare Part D.</strong> <a href="http://healthline.com//health/medicare/medicare-part-d" class="content-link css-kxhged">Medicare Part D</a> is prescription drug coverage. Part D plans are standalone plans that only cover prescriptions. These plans are also provided through private insurance companies.</li><li><strong>Medigap. </strong><a href="http://healthline.com/health/medicare/what-is-medigap" class="content-link css-kxhged">Medigap</a> is also known as Medicare supplement insurance. Medigap plans help cover the out-of-pocket costs of Medicare, like deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance amounts.</li></ul><p>Medicare Part A and Medicare Part B together are known as “original Medicare.” Original Medicare has a set standard for costs and coverage nationwide. That means your coverage will be the same no matter what state you live in, and you can use it in any state you visit.</p><p>Medicare Advantage plans, however, can be very different depending on where you live. Since these plans are offered by private companies, they have different price points and covered services depending on the plan and company you choose.</p><p>Many companies only serve their local area. Even large companies that offer plans throughout the country offer different plans in different states or even counties.</p><p>Unlike original Medicare, most Medicare Advantage plans also have a network you’ll need to stay in for coverage, especially if your plan is an HMO. Your plan builds a network of contracted healthcare providers, suppliers, and pharmacies in your area to provide a cost benefit.<br></p><h2><strong>What to look for in a plan</strong></h2><div class="css-1pkj7lb"><div class="css-zr4wb2"><div class="css-55guol"><h3 class="css-1v0jij4">Tips for selecting plans that meet your needs<br></h3><div class="css-ygw4tr"><ul class="pro-con--pro-list"><li><strong>Assess your current and potential healthcare needs.</strong> Are there doctors, facilities, or medications that you can't compromise on for your care? This may impact your policy choice, particularly when deciding between original Medicare and Medicare Advantage.</li><li><strong>Consider your income.</strong> If you have a fixed or limited income, paying monthly premiums may be difficult. However, if you may need care that only Medicare Advantage would cover, this might be a good option to save costs in the long run.</li><li><strong>Look for cost savings programs.</strong> You may qualify for certain programs to help with your costs, including<a href="https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/eligibility/index.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged"> Medicaid</a> and<a href="https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/help" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged"> Extra Help</a>.</li><li><strong>Find the right plan.</strong> Use Medicare’s <a href="https://www.medicare.gov/plan-compare/#/?lang=en" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">plan finder tool</a> to compare available Medicare Advantage plans in your area. You can search by prescription drugs you need, as well as covered providers and services.</li></ul></div></div> <div><div class="css-pzg5fr"></div></div></div> <div class="css-1enc0ig"><img decoding="async" src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Healthline_logo.svg/320px-Healthline_logo.svg.png" alt="Healthline" class="css-1tjsedf"></div></div><h2><strong>What differs by state</strong></h2><p>Medicare Advantage plans are offered by both local insurance companies and large national companies. No matter which company you go with, your plan will be specific to where you live.</p><p>Many plans are only available in a certain state, region, city, or even a single ZIP code. Even if the plan has the same name and covers the same services, your ZIP code could affect the price you pay.</p><p>Both Medicare Part D and Medigap plans work similarly. Like Medicare Advantage plans, they’re offered by private companies. You purchase them in addition to your original Medicare coverage, and the plans that are available to you will depend on where you live.</p><p>In general, plans in all states need to follow the same rules. For example, all Medicare Advantage plans must cover all the same services as original Medicare.</p><p>An exception to this is Medigap plans. In most states, Medigap plans will have the same letter names across all insurance companies and offer the same coverage. However, that’s not the case in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Massachusetts. All three of these states have their own Medigap regulations and plan types.</p><h2><strong>Medicare enrollment: When can I apply?</strong></h2><p>If you’re planning to enroll in Medicare, you'll need to know several <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/when-do-you-sign-up-for-medicare" class="content-link css-kxhged">enrollment deadlines</a> and dates:</p><ul><li><strong>Initial enrollment period.</strong> This is a 7-month window around your 65th birthday when you can sign up for Medicare. It begins 3 months before your birthday, includes the month of your birthday, and extends 3 months after your birthday. During this time, you can enroll for all parts of Medicare without a penalty.</li><li><strong>Open enrollment period (October 15–December 7).</strong> During this time, you can switch from original Medicare (parts A and B) to Part C (Medicare Advantage), or from Part C back to original Medicare. You can also switch Part C plans or add, remove, or change a Part D plan.</li><li><strong>General enrollment period (January 1–March 31).</strong> You can enroll in Medicare during this timeframe if you didn’t enroll during your initial enrollment period.</li><li><strong>Special enrollment period.</strong> If you delayed Medicare enrollment for an<a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-sign-up-period#special-enrollment-periods" class="content-link css-kxhged"> approved reason</a>, you can later enroll during a special enrollment period. You have 8 months from the end of your coverage or the end of your employment during which to sign up without penalty.</li><li><strong>Medicare Advantage open enrollment (January 1–March 31).</strong> During this period, you can switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another or go back to original Medicare. You cannot enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan if you currently have original Medicare.</li><li><strong>Part D enrollment/Medicare add-ons (April 1–June 30).</strong> If you don’t have Medicare Part A, but you enrolled in Part B during the general enrollment period, you can sign up for a Part D prescription drug plan..</li><li><strong>Medigap enrollment.</strong> This 6-month period starts after the first day of the month that you apply for original Medicare or from your 65th birthday. If you miss this enrollment period, you may not be able to get a Medigap plan. If you do get one later, you may pay higher premiums for it.</li></ul><div class="css-1pkj7lb"><div class="css-zr4wb2"><div class="css-55guol"><div class="css-ygw4tr"> The information on this website may assist you in making personal decisions about insurance, but it is not intended to provide advice regarding the purchase or use of any insurance or insurance products. Currently, the parts of Medicare include:\u003cbr\u003e"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedicare Part A.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-part-a\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eMedicare Part A\u003c/a\u003e is hospital insurance. It covers you during short-term, inpatient stays in hospitals and skilled nursing facilities or for some in-home services like limited home healthcare or hospice.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedicare Part B.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ca href=\"http://healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-part-b\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eMedicare Part B\u003c/a\u003e is medical insurance that covers everyday care needs like doctor\u0026apos;s appointments, therapist visits, medical equipment, and urgent care visits.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedicare Part C.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ca href=\"http://healthline.com//health/medicare/medicare-part-c\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eMedicare Part C\u003c/a\u003e is also called Medicare Advantage. These plans combine the coverage of parts A and B into a single plan. Medicare Advantage plans are offered by private insurance companies and are overseen by Medicare.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedicare Part D.\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ca href=\"http://healthline.com//health/medicare/medicare-part-d\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eMedicare Part D\u003c/a\u003e is prescription drug coverage. Part D plans are standalone plans that only cover prescriptions. These plans are also provided through private insurance companies.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedigap. \u003c/strong\u003e\u003ca href=\"http://healthline.com/health/medicare/what-is-medigap\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eMedigap\u003c/a\u003e is also known as Medicare supplement insurance. Medigap plans help cover the out-of-pocket costs of Medicare, like deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance amounts.\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Medicare Part A and Medicare Part B together are known as \u0026ldquo;original Medicare.\u0026rdquo; Original Medicare has a set standard for costs and coverage nationwide. That means your coverage will be the same no matter what state you live in, and you can use it in any state you visit."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Medicare Advantage plans, however, can be very different depending on where you live. Since these plans are offered by private companies, they have different price points and covered services depending on the plan and company you choose."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Many companies only serve their local area. Even large companies that offer plans throughout the country offer different plans in different states or even counties."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Unlike original Medicare, most Medicare Advantage plans also have a network you\u0026rsquo;ll need to stay in for coverage, especially if your plan is an HMO. Your plan builds a network of contracted healthcare providers, suppliers, and pharmacies in your area to provide a cost benefit.\u003cbr\u003e"},{"tagName":"h2","source":"\u003cstrong\u003eWhat to look for in a plan\u003c/strong\u003e"},{"tagName":"div","attributes":{"className":"css-1pkj7lb"},"source":"\u003cdiv class=\"css-zr4wb2\"\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"css-55guol\"\u003e\u003ch3 class=\"css-1v0jij4\"\u003eTips for selecting plans that meet your needs\u003cbr\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cdiv class=\"css-ygw4tr\"\u003e\u003cul class=\"pro-con--pro-list\"\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAssess your current and potential healthcare needs.\u003c/strong\u003e Are there doctors, facilities, or medications that you can\u0026apos;t compromise on for your care? This may impact your policy choice, particularly when deciding between original Medicare and Medicare Advantage.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eConsider your income.\u003c/strong\u003e If you have a fixed or limited income, paying monthly premiums may be difficult. However, if you may need care that only Medicare Advantage would cover, this might be a good option to save costs in the long run.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLook for cost savings programs.\u003c/strong\u003e You may qualify for certain programs to help with your costs, including\u003ca href=\"https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/eligibility/index.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003e Medicaid\u003c/a\u003e and\u003ca href=\"https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/help\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003e Extra Help\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eFind the right plan.\u003c/strong\u003e Use Medicare\u0026rsquo;s \u003ca href=\"https://www.medicare.gov/plan-compare/#/?lang=en\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eplan finder tool\u003c/a\u003e to compare available Medicare Advantage plans in your area. Even if the plan has the same name and covers the same services, your ZIP code could affect the price you pay."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Both Medicare Part D and Medigap plans work similarly. Like Medicare Advantage plans, they\u0026rsquo;re offered by private companies. You purchase them in addition to your original Medicare coverage, and the plans that are available to you will depend on where you live."},{"tagName":"p","source":"In general, plans in all states need to follow the same rules. For example, all Medicare Advantage plans must cover all the same services as original Medicare."},{"tagName":"p","source":"An exception to this is Medigap plans. In most states, Medigap plans will have the same letter names across all insurance companies and offer the same coverage. However, that\u0026rsquo;s not the case in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Massachusetts. All three of these states have their own Medigap regulations and plan types."},{"tagName":"h2","source":"\u003cstrong\u003eMedicare enrollment:\u0026nbsp;When can I apply?\u003c/strong\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"If you\u0026rsquo;re planning to enroll in Medicare, you\u0026apos;ll need to know several \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/when-do-you-sign-up-for-medicare\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eenrollment deadlines\u003c/a\u003e and dates:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eInitial enrollment period.\u003c/strong\u003e This is a 7-month window around your 65th birthday when you can sign up for Medicare. It begins 3 months before your birthday, includes the month of your birthday, and extends 3 months after your birthday. During this time, you can enroll for all parts of Medicare without a penalty.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eOpen enrollment period (October 15\u0026ndash;December 7).\u003c/strong\u003e During this time, you can switch from original Medicare (parts A and B) to Part C (Medicare Advantage), or from Part C back to original Medicare. You can also switch Part C plans or add, remove, or change a Part D plan.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eGeneral enrollment period (January 1\u0026ndash;March 31).\u003c/strong\u003e You can enroll in Medicare during this timeframe if you didn\u0026rsquo;t enroll during your initial enrollment period.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSpecial enrollment period.\u003c/strong\u003e If you delayed Medicare enrollment for an\u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/medicare/medicare-sign-up-period#special-enrollment-periods\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003e approved reason\u003c/a\u003e, you can later enroll during a special enrollment period. You have 8 months from the end of your coverage or the end of your employment during which to sign up without penalty.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedicare Advantage open enrollment (January 1\u0026ndash;March 31).\u003c/strong\u003e During this period, you can switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another or go back to original Medicare. You cannot enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan if you currently have original Medicare.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePart D enrollment/Medicare add-ons (April 1\u0026ndash;June 30).\u003c/strong\u003e If you don\u0026rsquo;t have Medicare Part A, but you enrolled in Part B during the general enrollment period, you can sign up for a Part D prescription drug plan..\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eMedigap enrollment.\u003c/strong\u003e This 6-month period starts after the first day of the month that you apply for original Medicare or from your 65th birthday. If you miss this enrollment period, you may not be able to get a Medigap plan. Search for medicare plans in your state Select your state Alabama Alaska Arizona Arkansas California Colorado Connecticut Delaware Florida Georgia Hawaii Idaho Illinois Indiana Iowa Kansas Kentucky Louisiana Maine Maryland Massachusetts Michigan Minnesota Mississippi Missouri Montana Nebraska Nevada New Hampshire New Jersey New Mexico New York North Carolina North Dakota Ohio Oklahoma Oregon Pennsylvania Rhode Island South Carolina South Dakota Tennessee Texas Utah Vermont Virginia Washington West Virginia Wisconsin Wyoming Medicare overview Medicare is a government-funded health insurance program that provides medical coverage for people ages 65 or older. You can also qualify if you have certain health conditions or disabilities . Medicare is divided into a few “parts.” Each part of Medicare covers different healthcare needs. Currently, the parts of Medicare include: Medicare Part A. Medicare Part A is hospital insurance. It covers you during short-term, inpatient stays in hospitals and skilled nursing facilities or for some in-home services like limited home healthcare or hospice. Medicare Part B. Medicare Part B is medical insurance that covers everyday care needs like doctor's appointments, therapist visits, medical equipment, and urgent care visits. Medicare Part C. Medicare Part C is also called Medicare Advantage. These plans combine the coverage of parts A and B into a single plan. Medicare Advantage plans are offered by private insurance companies and are overseen by Medicare. Medicare Part D. Medicare Part D is prescription drug coverage. Part D plans are standalone plans that only cover prescriptions. These plans are also provided through private insurance companies. Medigap. Medigap is also known as Medicare supplement insurance. Medigap plans help cover the out-of-pocket costs of Medicare, like deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance amounts. Medicare Part A and Medicare Part B together are known as “original Medicare.” Original Medicare has a set standard for costs and coverage nationwide. That means your coverage will be the same no matter what state you live in, and you can use it in any state you visit. Medicare Advantage plans, however, can be very different depending on where you live. Since these plans are offered by private companies, they have different price points and covered services depending on the plan and company you choose. Many companies only serve their local area. Even large companies that offer plans throughout the country offer different plans in different states or even counties. Unlike original Medicare, most Medicare Advantage plans also have a network you’ll need to stay in for coverage, especially if your plan is an HMO. Your plan builds a network of contracted healthcare providers, suppliers, and pharmacies in your area to provide a cost benefit. What to look for in a plan Tips for selecting plans that meet your needs Assess your current and potential healthcare needs. Are there doctors, facilities, or medications that you can't compromise on for your care? This may impact your policy choice, particularly when deciding between original Medicare and Medicare Advantage. Consider your income. If you have a fixed or limited income, paying monthly premiums may be difficult. However, if you may need care that only Medicare Advantage would cover, this might be a good option to save costs in the long run. Look for cost savings programs. You may qualify for certain programs to help with your costs, including Medicaid and Extra Help . Find the right plan. Use Medicare’s plan finder tool to compare available Medicare Advantage plans in your area. You can search by prescription drugs you need, as well as covered providers and services. What differs by state Medicare Advantage plans are offered by both local insurance companies and large national companies. No matter which company you go with, your plan will be specific to where you live. Many plans are only available in a certain state, region, city, or even a single ZIP code. Even if the plan has the same name and covers the same services, your ZIP code could affect the price you pay. Both Medicare Part D and Medigap plans work similarly. Like Medicare Advantage plans, they’re offered by private companies. You purchase them in addition to your original Medicare coverage, and the plans that are available to you will depend on where you live. In general, plans in all states need to follow the same rules. For example, all Medicare Advantage plans must cover all the same services as original Medicare. An exception to this is Medigap plans. In most states, Medigap plans will have the same letter names across all insurance companies and offer the same coverage. However, that’s not the case in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Massachusetts. All three of these states have their own Medigap regulations and plan types. Medicare enrollment: When can I apply? If you’re planning to enroll in Medicare, you'll need to know several enrollment deadlines and dates: Initial enrollment period. This is a 7-month window around your 65th birthday when you can sign up for Medicare. It begins 3 months before your birthday, includes the month of your birthday, and extends 3 months after your birthday. During this time, you can enroll for all parts of Medicare without a penalty. Open enrollment period (October 15–December 7). During this time, you can switch from original Medicare (parts A and B) to Part C (Medicare Advantage), or from Part C back to original Medicare. You can also switch Part C plans or add, remove, or change a Part D plan. General enrollment period (January 1–March 31). You can enroll in Medicare during this timeframe if you didn’t enroll during your initial enrollment period. Special enrollment period. If you delayed Medicare enrollment for an approved reason , you can later enroll during a special enrollment period. You have 8 months from the end of your coverage or the end of your employment during which to sign up without penalty. Medicare Advantage open enrollment (January 1–March 31). During this period, you can switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another or go back to original Medicare. You cannot enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan if you currently have original Medicare. Part D enrollment/Medicare add-ons (April 1–June 30). If you don’t have Medicare Part A, but you enrolled in Part B during the general enrollment period, you can sign up for a Part D prescription drug plan.. Medigap enrollment. This 6-month period starts after the first day of the month that you apply for original Medicare or from your 65th birthday. If you miss this enrollment period, you may not be able to get a Medigap plan. If you do get one later, you may pay higher premiums for it. class="css-clxyy9"><span></span><div><div data-testid="widget" data-widget="108976-tabbed-content-block"><div class="css-mqvucf"><div class="css-1k4tg43" data-testid="action-guides-tabbed"><article data-variant="tilesNoTabs" aria-label="Key takeaways" class="css-1e96uhg"><header><h2 class="css-ba3xht">Key takeaways</h2><div class="css-t9podz"><ul>
<li>Radiation therapy takes high-energy rays to target and slow the growth of breast cancer cells. It’s often used post-surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence.</li>



<li>External beam radiation targets the tumor site using a machine, while internal radiation (brachytherapy) involves placing a radioactive source inside the breast.</li>



<li>Common side effects of radiation may include skin irritation, fatigue, and breast swelling. You can manage these with rest, proper skin care, and loose-fitting clothing.</li>
</ul></div></header><section></section></article></div></div></div></div><div><p>Breast cancer can be treated in a variety of ways, including with <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/radiation-therapy" class="content-link css-kxhged">radiation therapy</a>. </p></div><div><div data-preamp="serena-chatbot"></div></div><div><p>Depending on the type and stage of breast cancer, radiation can be used alone or combined with other therapies.</p></div><div><p>There are multiple types of radiation therapy for breast cancer and different schedules for radiation treatments. Read on to learn how to prepare for this treatment. </p></div><div class="css-168l8xe"><aside class="css-zezy6m" data-testid="sticky-inline-ad" data-sticky="false"><div class="css-1xdhyk6"><div class="css-1v9qaky" data-empty="true"><div class="css-111xg9d"><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div id="inline2__slot" data-adbridg-ad-class="inline2__slot" data-ad="true" data-adbridg-skvp="" class="css-fo4nvu"></div></div></div></aside></div></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="about" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="about">What is radiation therapy?</a></div></h2></div><span style="font-size:0;line-height:0"></span><div><p>According to the <hl-trusted-source source="National Cancer Institute " rationale="Governmental authority"><a href="https://www.cancer.gov/publications/patient-education/radiationttherapy.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">National Cancer Institute</a></hl-trusted-source>, radiation therapy uses high energy rays or particles to kill cancer cells. </p></div><div><p>Radiation kills or slows the growth of cancer cells. It also affects nearby healthy cells, but the healthy cells typically recover after the course of radiation treatment has ended. Doctors try to protect healthy cells by:</p></div><div><ul><li>using as low a dose of radiation as possible </li><li>spreading out treatment over time</li><li>aiming the radiation at a very specific part of your body</li></ul></div><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="when-its-used" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="when-its-used">When is radiation used for breast cancer?</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Radiation therapy can be used in a variety of instances for breast cancer treatment. It can be used:</p></div><div><ul><li>after <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/breast-lump-removal" class="content-link css-kxhged">breast-conserving surgery</a>, to reduce the risk of recurrence in your breast</li><li>after a <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/modified-radical-mastectomy" class="content-link css-kxhged">mastectomy</a>, particularly if: <ul><li>the tumor was larger than 5 centimeters </li><li>there was cancer in your lymph nodes</li><li>the margins were positive </li></ul></li><li>to help ease side effects if the cancer spreads to other areas of your body, such as your bones or brain</li></ul></div><div><p>Depending on the type of breast cancer and the cancer stage, radiation may be used in combination with other cancer treatments, such as surgery and <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/chemotherapy" class="content-link css-kxhged">chemotherapy</a>.</p></div><div class="css-168l8xe"><aside class="css-zezy6m" data-testid="sticky-inline-ad" data-sticky="false"><div class="css-1xdhyk6"><div class="css-1v9qaky" data-empty="true"><div class="css-111xg9d"><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div id="inline7__slot" data-adbridg-ad-class="inline7__slot" data-ad="true" data-adbridg-skvp="" class="css-fo4nvu"></div></div></div></aside></div></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="types" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="types">What types of radiation therapy are used for breast cancer?</a></div></h2></div><div><p>There are two main types of radiation therapy: external beam radiation and internal radiation. Some people receive both types of treatment. </p></div><div><h3>External beam radiation</h3></div><div><p>External beam radiation is the <hl-trusted-source source="American Cancer Society" rationale="Highly respected international organization"><a href="https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/treatment-types/radiation/external-beam-radiation-therapy.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">most common</a></hl-trusted-source> type of radiation therapy for breast cancer.</p></div><div><p>During this treatment, a large machine sends beams of radiation to the area of your breast that is affected by cancer. </p></div><div><p>The beams are aimed directly at the site of your tumor. While the machine moves around you, it can send radiation to your tumor from different directions.</p></div><div><h3>Internal radiation</h3></div><div><p>Internal radiation <hl-trusted-source source="American Cancer Society" rationale="Highly respected international organization"><a href="https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/treatment-types/radiation/internal-radiation-therapy-brachytherapy.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">involves</a></hl-trusted-source> putting a source of radiation into your body. This type of radiation treatment is also known as <a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/cancer/brachytherapy" class="content-link css-kxhged">brachytherapy</a>. </p></div><div><p>For this treatment, healthcare professionals will temporarily place a device with radioactive seeds or pellets into your breast tissue in the area where the tumor was located. To treat breast cancer, internal radiation is often given through one or more catheters (small tubes).</p></div><div><p>Some factors, such as the size and location of the tumor, can limit who can receive this type of radiation therapy. </p></div><div><p>Internal radiation typically works well when:</p></div><div><ul><li>breast cancer is in an early stage </li><li>cancer is present in just one spot in your breast</li><li>you’ve had breast-conserving surgery</li></ul></div><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="what-to-expect" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="what-to-expect">What can you expect when you have radiation therapy?</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Knowing what to expect before radiation therapy can help you better prepare for the treatment and address any concerns you might have ahead of time.</p></div><div><h3>What to expect with external beam radiation</h3></div><div><p>If you receive external beam radiation, you’ll meet with your radiation oncologist and a nurse before starting treatment. They will walk you through what to expect during external beam radiation, as well as the risks and benefits of this treatment. </p></div><div><p>At that time, you’ll likely have a physical exam and go over your medical history. </p></div><div><p>Additionally, the radiation oncologist and a radiation therapist will take scans of your treatment area. This will help them define the boundaries of the affected area so they know where to aim the radiation beams. </p></div><div><p>They will put marks (tattoos or ink) on your skin to identify the area. You’ll need the marks throughout the course of your treatment. Healthcare professionals will use the marks to line up your body so that the radiation beams target the exact area that needs to be treated. </p></div><div><p>In some cases, healthcare professionals may make a body mold to help keep you still during the treatment.</p></div><div><p>Each treatment will last only a few minutes. In fact, the session setup will take longer than the actual treatment. You won’t feel anything when the machine is turned on for the treatment. It is a painless procedure. </p></div><div><h3>What to expect with internal radiation</h3></div><div><p>Before you get any internal radiation, you’ll meet with your radiation oncologist. They will:</p></div><div><ul><li>perform a physical exam</li><li>ask about your medical history</li><li>go over what your internal radiation treatment will involve</li></ul></div><div><p>Most internal radiation is given through a catheter. This is a small, flexible tube that’s surgically placed into the space that’s left after breast-conserving surgery. </p></div><div><p>At the end of the catheter is a device that can be inflated inside your breast so that it stays in place for the duration of the treatment. </p></div><div><p>During your treatment, a healthcare professional will insert radiation pellets or seeds through the catheter and into the inflatable device. The pellets will usually stay there for 10 to 20 minutes or longer, and then the healthcare professional will remove them. How long the radiation pellets stay in place depends on:</p></div><div><ul><li>your type of cancer</li><li>your overall health</li><li>other cancer treatments you’ve had</li></ul></div><div><p>Once the course of treatment is over, healthcare professionals will remove the catheter and the inflatable device.</p></div><div class="css-168l8xe"><aside class="css-zezy6m" data-testid="sticky-inline-ad" data-sticky="false"><div class="css-1xdhyk6"><div class="css-1v9qaky" data-empty="true"><div class="css-111xg9d"><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div id="inline12__slot" data-adbridg-ad-class="inline12__slot" data-ad="true" data-adbridg-skvp="" class="css-fo4nvu"></div></div></div></aside></div></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="treatment-duration" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="treatment-duration">How long does radiation therapy typically last?</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Radiation therapy usually begins <a href="https://cancer.ca/en/cancer-information/cancer-types/breast/treatment/radiation-therapy" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">3 to 4 weeks</a> after a breast-conserving surgery or a mastectomy. </p></div><div><p>External beam radiation is typically given once per day, 5 days per week, for <hl-trusted-source source="National Cancer Institute " rationale="Governmental authority"><a href="https://www.cancer.gov/publications/patient-education/radiation-therapy-and-you.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="content-link css-kxhged">2 to 10 weeks</a></hl-trusted-source> on an outpatient basis. This means you can go home after the treatment.</p></div><div><p>The schedule for external radiation may differ from the standard schedule in cases such as the following:</p></div><div><ul><li><strong>Accelerated fractionation:</strong> Treatment is given in larger daily or weekly doses, reducing the duration of the treatment.</li><li><strong>Hyperfractionation:</strong> Smaller doses of radiation are given more than once per day. </li><li><strong>Hypofractionation:</strong> Larger doses of radiation are given once daily (or less often) to reduce the number of treatments. </li></ul></div><div><p>For internal radiation, treatments are usually given twice per day for 5 days in a row as outpatient procedures. Your specific treatment schedule will depend on what your oncologist has ordered.</p></div><div><p>A less common treatment option is to leave the radiation in your body for hours or days. During this type of treatment, you’ll stay in the hospital to protect others from the radiation.</p></div><span class="css-ryxryr"></span></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="side-effects" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="side-effects">What are the side effects?</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Common side effects of external beam radiation therapy for breast cancer include:</p></div><div><ul><li>sunburn-like skin irritation in the treatment area </li><li>dry, itchy, tender skin </li><li><a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/fatigue" class="content-link css-kxhged">fatigue</a></li><li>swelling or heaviness in your breast</li></ul></div><div><p>Skin changes and changes to your breast tissue usually go away within a few months to a year.</p></div><div><p>Hair loss from radiation typically occurs only in areas that are radiated. If you receive external beam radiation to your breast, you typically won’t lose your hair on your head. You may lose hair in your armpits, depending on the area being radiated.</p></div><div><p>External beam radiation can also have long-term effects, which may:</p></div><div><ul><li>cause your breast to become smaller and harder</li><li>make breastfeeding more difficult</li><li>affect your reconstruction options</li><li>affect nerves in your arm</li></ul></div><div><p>Internal radiation typically has fewer side effects than external beam radiation. The most common side effects are:</p></div><div><ul><li>redness or other skin color changes and bruising</li><li>breast pain</li><li><a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/infections#1" class="content-link css-kxhged">infection</a></li><li><a href="https://www.healthline.com/health/fat-necrosis-breast" class="content-link css-kxhged">fatty tissue damage</a></li><li>fluid buildup in your breast</li><li>weakness in and fractures of your ribs (in rare cases)</li></ul></div></div><div data-testid="tabbed-article-section" data-section-id="managing-side-effects" class="css-1xdhyk6"><span></span><div><h2><div><a class="chartbeat-section" name="managing-side-effects">Managing side effects</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Many side effects of radiation go away within a few months of the end of your treatment. There are steps you can take to help minimize some of the side effects. </p></div><div><div data-testid="widget" data-widget="108977-widget-call-out"><div id="widget_call_out_59fe2427-5c03-47e6-8b5c-7d57b8e2f36c" data-widget-position="106305" class="css-1wyihkl"><span style="font-size:0;line-height:0;margin-top:-100px"></span><div class="css-c0yr9y"><div class="css-1onfw7d"><h3 class="css-9wz6ku">Ways to minimize side effects</h3><div class="css-uex56a"><ul><li>Fatigue can last long after radiation therapy has ended. Be sure to get plenty of rest, eat a balanced diet, <a href="https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/how-much-water-should-you-drink-per-day" class="content-link css-kxhged">stay hydrated</a>, exercise regularly, and keep a log of your fatigue so you can give your doctor an accurate account of this side effect.</li><li>Use only lotion and other skin products that your doctor recommends.</li><li>Avoid putting anything too hot or too cold on your affected skin.</li><li>Wear loose-fitting clothes that won’t rub against your skin.</li><li>Avoid tanning beds. The UV rays can further irritate and inflame your skin.</li><li>Avoid sun exposure on the treatment area.</li><li>Don’t use deodorants, perfumes, or products that contain alcohol unless your doctor name="takeaway">Takeaway</a></div></h2></div><div><p>Radiation therapy for breast cancer is a common treatment that kills or slows the growth of cancer cells. While it also affects nearby healthy cells, these cells usually recover after the treatment ends. </p></div><div><p>Radiation therapy can be used alone or with other treatments, such as surgery and chemotherapy. </p></div><div><p>Two common types of radiation treatment for breast cancer are external beam radiation and internal radiation, which is also known as brachytherapy. Internal radiation typically has fewer side effects. </p></div><div><p>The type of radiation that’s best suited for you depends on:</p></div><div><ul><li>the type and stage of your breast cancer</li><li>your overall health</li><li>other cancer treatments you’ve had</li></ul></div><div><p>Talk with your doctor about your treatment options. "}]},{"id":"about","title":"About ","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["What is radiation therapy?"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"According to the \u003chl-trusted-source source=\"National Cancer Institute \" rationale=\"Governmental authority\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.cancer.gov/publications/patient-education/radiationttherapy.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003eNational Cancer Institute\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/hl-trusted-source\u003e, radiation therapy uses high energy rays or particles to kill cancer cells. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"Radiation kills or slows the growth of cancer cells. It also affects nearby healthy cells, but the healthy cells typically recover after the course of radiation treatment has ended. Doctors try to protect healthy cells by:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003eusing as low a dose of radiation as possible \u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003espreading out treatment over time\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eaiming the radiation at a very specific part of your body\u003c/li\u003e"}]},{"id":"when-its-used","title":"When it’s used","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["When is radiation used for breast cancer?"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"Radiation therapy can be used in a variety of instances for breast cancer treatment. It can be used:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003eafter \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/breast-lump-removal\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003ebreast-conserving surgery\u003c/a\u003e, to reduce the risk of recurrence in your breast\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eafter a \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/modified-radical-mastectomy\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003emastectomy\u003c/a\u003e, particularly if: \u003cul\u003e\u003cli\u003ethe tumor was larger than 5 centimeters \u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ethere was cancer in your lymph nodes\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ethe margins were positive \u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eto help ease side effects if the cancer spreads to other areas of your body, such as your bones or brain\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Depending on the type of breast cancer and the cancer stage, radiation may be used in combination with other cancer treatments, such as surgery and \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/chemotherapy\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003echemotherapy\u003c/a\u003e."}]},{"id":"types","title":"Types","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["What types of radiation therapy are used for breast cancer?"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"There are two main types of radiation therapy: external beam radiation and internal radiation. Some people receive both types of treatment. "},{"tagName":"h3","source":"External beam radiation"},{"tagName":"p","source":"External beam radiation is the \u003chl-trusted-source source=\"American Cancer Society\" rationale=\"Highly respected international organization\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/treatment-types/radiation/external-beam-radiation-therapy.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003emost common\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/hl-trusted-source\u003e type of radiation therapy for breast cancer."},{"tagName":"p","source":"During this treatment, a large machine sends beams of radiation to the area of your breast that is affected by cancer. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"The beams are aimed directly at the site of your tumor. While the machine moves around you, it can send radiation to your tumor from different directions."},{"tagName":"h3","source":"Internal radiation"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Internal radiation \u003chl-trusted-source source=\"American Cancer Society\" rationale=\"Highly respected international organization\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/treatment-types/radiation/internal-radiation-therapy-brachytherapy.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003einvolves\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/hl-trusted-source\u003e putting a source of radiation into your body. This type of radiation treatment is also known as \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/cancer/brachytherapy\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003ebrachytherapy\u003c/a\u003e. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"For this treatment, healthcare professionals will temporarily place a device with radioactive seeds or pellets into your breast tissue in the area where the tumor was located. To treat breast cancer, internal radiation is often given through one or more catheters (small tubes)."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Some factors, such as the size and location of the tumor, can limit who can receive this type of radiation therapy. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"Internal radiation typically works well when:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003ebreast cancer is in an early stage \u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ecancer is present in just one spot in your breast\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eyou’ve had breast-conserving surgery\u003c/li\u003e"}]},{"id":"what-to-expect","title":"What to expect","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["What can you expect when you have radiation therapy?"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"Knowing what to expect before radiation therapy can help you better prepare for the treatment and address any concerns you might have ahead of time."},{"tagName":"h3","source":"What to expect with external beam radiation"},{"tagName":"p","source":"If you receive external beam radiation, you’ll meet with your radiation oncologist and a nurse before starting treatment. They will walk you through what to expect during external beam radiation, as well as the risks and benefits of this treatment. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"At that time, you’ll likely have a physical exam and go over your medical history. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"Additionally, the radiation oncologist and a radiation therapist will take scans of your treatment area. This will help them define the boundaries of the affected area so they know where to aim the radiation beams. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"They will put marks (tattoos or ink) on your skin to identify the area. You’ll need the marks throughout the course of your treatment. Healthcare professionals will use the marks to line up your body so that the radiation beams target the exact area that needs to be treated. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"In some cases, healthcare professionals may make a body mold to help keep you still during the treatment."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Each treatment will last only a few minutes. In fact, the session setup will take longer than the actual treatment. You won’t feel anything when the machine is turned on for the treatment. It is a painless procedure. "},{"tagName":"h3","source":"What to expect with internal radiation"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Before you get any internal radiation, you’ll meet with your radiation oncologist. They will:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003eperform a physical exam\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eask about your medical history\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ego over what your internal radiation treatment will involve\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Most internal radiation is given through a catheter. This is a small, flexible tube that’s surgically placed into the space that’s left after breast-conserving surgery. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"At the end of the catheter is a device that can be inflated inside your breast so that it stays in place for the duration of the treatment. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"During your treatment, a healthcare professional will insert radiation pellets or seeds through the catheter and into the inflatable device. The pellets will usually stay there for 10 to 20 minutes or longer, and then the healthcare professional will remove them. How long the radiation pellets stay in place depends on:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003eyour type of cancer\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eyour overall health\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eother cancer treatments you’ve had\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Once the course of treatment is over, healthcare professionals will remove the catheter and the inflatable device."}]},{"id":"treatment-duration","title":"Treatment duration","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["How long does radiation therapy typically last?"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"Radiation therapy usually begins \u003ca href=\"https://cancer.ca/en/cancer-information/cancer-types/breast/treatment/radiation-therapy\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003e3 to 4 weeks\u003c/a\u003e after a breast-conserving surgery or a mastectomy. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"External beam radiation is typically given once per day, 5 days per week, for \u003chl-trusted-source source=\"National Cancer Institute \" rationale=\"Governmental authority\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.cancer.gov/publications/patient-education/radiation-therapy-and-you.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003e2 to 10 weeks\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/hl-trusted-source\u003e on an outpatient basis. This means you can go home after the treatment."},{"tagName":"p","source":"The schedule for external radiation may differ from the standard schedule in cases such as the following:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAccelerated fractionation:\u003c/strong\u003e Treatment is given in larger daily or weekly doses, reducing the duration of the treatment.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHyperfractionation:\u003c/strong\u003e Smaller doses of radiation are given more than once per day. \u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eHypofractionation:\u003c/strong\u003e Larger doses of radiation are given once daily (or less often) to reduce the number of treatments. \u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"For internal radiation, treatments are usually given twice per day for 5 days in a row as outpatient procedures. Your specific treatment schedule will depend on what your oncologist has ordered."},{"tagName":"p","source":"A less common treatment option is to leave the radiation in your body for hours or days. During this type of treatment, you’ll stay in the hospital to protect others from the radiation."}]},{"id":"side-effects","title":"Side effects","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["What are the side effects?"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"Common side effects of external beam radiation therapy for breast cancer include:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003esunburn-like skin irritation in the treatment area \u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003edry, itchy, tender skin \u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/fatigue\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003efatigue\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eswelling or heaviness in your breast\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Skin changes and changes to your breast tissue usually go away within a few months to a year."},{"tagName":"p","source":"Hair loss from radiation typically occurs only in areas that are radiated. If you receive external beam radiation to your breast, you typically won’t lose your hair on your head. You may lose hair in your armpits, depending on the area being radiated."},{"tagName":"p","source":"External beam radiation can also have long-term effects, which may:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003ecause your breast to become smaller and harder\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003emake breastfeeding more difficult\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eaffect your reconstruction options\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eaffect nerves in your arm\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Internal radiation typically has fewer side effects than external beam radiation. The most common side effects are:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003eredness or other skin color changes and bruising\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003ebreast pain\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/infections#1\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003einfection\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/health/fat-necrosis-breast\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003efatty tissue damage\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003efluid buildup in your breast\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eweakness in and fractures of your ribs (in rare cases)\u003c/li\u003e"}]},{"id":"managing-side-effects","title":"Managing side effects","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["Managing side effects"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"Many side effects of radiation go away within a few months of the end of your treatment. There are steps you can take to help minimize some of the side effects. "},{"widget":{"widgetFormat":"widget-call-out","items":[{"isBullets":true,"list":true,"standoutVariant":"general","headerTitle":["Ways to minimize side effects"],"content":[{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003eFatigue can last long after radiation therapy has ended. Be sure to get plenty of rest, eat a balanced diet, \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/how-much-water-should-you-drink-per-day\" class=\"content-link css-kxhged\"\u003estay hydrated\u003c/a\u003e, exercise regularly, and keep a log of your fatigue so you can give your doctor an accurate account of this side effect.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eUse only lotion and other skin products that your doctor recommends.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAvoid putting anything too hot or too cold on your affected skin.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eWear loose-fitting clothes that won’t rub against your skin.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAvoid tanning beds. The UV rays can further irritate and inflame your skin.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eAvoid sun exposure on the treatment area.\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eDon’t use deodorants, perfumes, or products that contain alcohol unless your doctor tells you it’s safe to do so.\u003c/li\u003e"}]}]},"brandPage":{}},{"tagName":"p","source":"If you have persistent side effects, talk with your doctor. "}]},{"id":"takeaway","title":"Takeaway","isCollapsable":false,"listicleSection":false,"header":["Takeaway"],"body":[{"tagName":"p","source":"Radiation therapy for breast cancer is a common treatment that kills or slows the growth of cancer cells. While it also affects nearby healthy cells, these cells usually recover after the treatment ends. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"Radiation therapy can be used alone or with other treatments, such as surgery and chemotherapy. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"Two common types of radiation treatment for breast cancer are external beam radiation and internal radiation, which is also known as brachytherapy. Internal radiation typically has fewer side effects. "},{"tagName":"p","source":"The type of radiation that’s best suited for you depends on:"},{"tagName":"ul","source":"\u003cli\u003ethe type and stage of your breast cancer\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eyour overall health\u003c/li\u003e\u003cli\u003eother cancer treatments you’ve had\u003c/li\u003e"},{"tagName":"p","source":"Talk with your doctor about your treatment options. on August 15, 2024 About When it’s used Types What to expect Treatment duration Side effects Managing side effects Takeaway Key takeaways Radiation therapy takes high-energy rays to target and slow the growth of breast cancer cells. It’s often used post-surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence. External beam radiation targets the tumor site using a machine, while internal radiation (brachytherapy) involves placing a radioactive source inside the breast. Common side effects of radiation may include skin irritation, fatigue, and breast swelling. You can manage these with rest, proper skin care, and loose-fitting clothing. Breast cancer can be treated in a variety of ways, including with radiation therapy . Depending on the type and stage of breast cancer, radiation can be used alone or combined with other therapies. There are multiple types of radiation therapy for breast cancer and different schedules for radiation treatments. Read on to learn how to prepare for this treatment. What is radiation therapy? According to the National Cancer Institute , radiation therapy uses high energy rays or particles to kill cancer cells. Radiation kills or slows the growth of cancer cells. It also affects nearby healthy cells, but the healthy cells typically recover after the course of radiation treatment has ended. Doctors try to protect healthy cells by: using as low a dose of radiation as possible spreading out treatment over time aiming the radiation at a very specific part of your body When is radiation used for breast cancer? Radiation therapy can be used in a variety of instances for breast cancer treatment. It can be used: after breast-conserving surgery , to reduce the risk of recurrence in your breast after a mastectomy , particularly if: the tumor was larger than 5 centimeters there was cancer in your lymph nodes the margins were positive to help ease side effects if the cancer spreads to other areas of your body, such as your bones or brain Depending on the type of breast cancer and the cancer stage, radiation may be used in combination with other cancer treatments, such as surgery and chemotherapy . What types of radiation therapy are used for breast cancer? There are two main types of radiation therapy: external beam radiation and internal radiation. Some people receive both types of treatment. External beam radiation External beam radiation is the most common type of radiation therapy for breast cancer. During this treatment, a large machine sends beams of radiation to the area of your breast that is affected by cancer. The beams are aimed directly at the site of your tumor. While the machine moves around you, it can send radiation to your tumor from different directions. Internal radiation Internal radiation involves putting a source of radiation into your body. This type of radiation treatment is also known as brachytherapy . For this treatment, healthcare professionals will temporarily place a device with radioactive seeds or pellets into your breast tissue in the area where the tumor was located. To treat breast cancer, internal radiation is often given through one or more catheters (small tubes). Some factors, such as the size and location of the tumor, can limit who can receive this type of radiation therapy. Internal radiation typically works well when: breast cancer is in an early stage cancer is present in just one spot in your breast you’ve had breast-conserving surgery What can you expect when you have radiation therapy? Knowing what to expect before radiation therapy can help you better prepare for the treatment and address any concerns you might have ahead of time. What to expect with external beam radiation If you receive external beam radiation, you’ll meet with your radiation oncologist and a nurse before starting treatment. They will walk you through what to expect during external beam radiation, as well as the risks and benefits of this treatment. At that time, you’ll likely have a physical exam and go over your medical history. Additionally, the radiation oncologist and a radiation therapist will take scans of your treatment area. This will help them define the boundaries of the affected area so they know where to aim the radiation beams. They will put marks (tattoos or ink) on your skin to identify the area. You’ll need the marks throughout the course of your treatment. Healthcare professionals will use the marks to line up your body so that the radiation beams target the exact area that needs to be treated. In some cases, healthcare professionals may make a body mold to help keep you still during the treatment. Each treatment will last only a few minutes. In fact, the session setup will take longer than the actual treatment. You won’t feel anything when the machine is turned on for the treatment. It is a painless procedure. What to expect with internal radiation Before you get any internal radiation, you’ll meet with your radiation oncologist. They will: perform a physical exam ask about your medical history go over what your internal radiation treatment will involve Most internal radiation is given through a catheter. This is a small, flexible tube that’s surgically placed into the space that’s left after breast-conserving surgery. At the end of the catheter is a device that can be inflated inside your breast so that it stays in place for the duration of the treatment. During your treatment, a healthcare professional will insert radiation pellets or seeds through the catheter and into the inflatable device. The pellets will usually stay there for 10 to 20 minutes or longer, and then the healthcare professional will remove them. How long the radiation pellets stay in place depends on: your type of cancer your overall health other cancer treatments you’ve had Once the course of treatment is over, healthcare professionals will remove the catheter and the inflatable device. How long does radiation therapy typically last? Radiation therapy usually begins 3 to 4 weeks after a breast-conserving surgery or a mastectomy. External beam radiation is typically given once per day, 5 days per week, for 2 to 10 weeks on an outpatient basis. This means you can go home after the treatment. The schedule for external radiation may differ from the standard schedule in cases such as the following: Accelerated fractionation: Treatment is given in larger daily or weekly doses, reducing the duration of the treatment. Hyperfractionation: Smaller doses of radiation are given more than once per day. Hypofractionation: Larger doses of radiation are given once daily (or less often) to reduce the number of treatments. For internal radiation, treatments are usually given twice per day for 5 days in a row as outpatient procedures. Your specific treatment schedule will depend on what your oncologist has ordered. A less common treatment option is to leave the radiation in your body for hours or days. During this type of treatment, you’ll stay in the hospital to protect others from the radiation. What are the side effects? Common side effects of external beam radiation therapy for breast cancer include: sunburn-like skin irritation in the treatment area dry, itchy, tender skin fatigue swelling or heaviness in your breast Skin changes and changes to your breast tissue usually go away within a few months to a year. Hair loss from radiation typically occurs only in areas that are radiated. If you receive external beam radiation to your breast, you typically won’t lose your hair on your head. You may lose hair in your armpits, depending on the area being radiated. External beam radiation can also have long-term effects, which may: cause your breast to become smaller and harder make breastfeeding more difficult affect your reconstruction options affect nerves in your arm Internal radiation typically has fewer side effects than external beam radiation. The most common side effects are: redness or other skin color changes and bruising breast pain infection fatty tissue damage fluid buildup in your breast weakness in and fractures of your ribs (in rare cases) Managing side effects Many side effects of radiation go away within a few months of the end of your treatment. There are steps you can take to help minimize some of the side effects. Ways to minimize side effects Fatigue can last long after radiation therapy has ended. Be sure to get plenty of rest, eat a balanced diet, stay hydrated , exercise regularly, and keep a log of your fatigue so you can give your doctor an accurate account of this side effect. Use only lotion and other skin products that your doctor recommends. Avoid putting anything too hot or too cold on your affected skin. Wear loose-fitting clothes that won’t rub against your skin. Avoid tanning beds. The UV rays can further irritate and inflame your skin. Avoid sun exposure on the treatment area. Don’t use deodorants, perfumes, or products that contain alcohol unless your doctor tells you it’s safe to do so. If you have persistent side effects, talk with your doctor. Takeaway Radiation therapy for breast cancer is a common treatment that kills or slows the growth of cancer cells. While it also affects nearby healthy cells, these cells usually recover after the treatment ends. Radiation therapy can be used alone or with other treatments, such as surgery and chemotherapy. Two common types of radiation treatment for breast cancer are external beam radiation and internal radiation, which is also known as brachytherapy. Internal radiation typically has fewer side effects. The type of radiation that’s best suited for you depends on: the type and stage of your breast cancer your overall health other cancer treatments you’ve had Talk with your doctor about your treatment options. Together, you can make the treatment decisions that are right for you.
